nameStory: Water lettuce gets its name from its rosette of pale green leaves that look remarkably like a floating head of lettuce bobbing on the water's surface. The leaves are arranged in a circular pattern just like lettuce leaves, and they have that same crisp, fresh appearance that makes you think of a garden salad floating in a pond!
description: Water lettuce is a free-floating aquatic plant that looks exactly like its name suggests - a head of lettuce drifting on the water. This tropical plant forms rosettes of thick, velvety leaves that can grow 4-6 inches across, with feathery white roots dangling beneath like underwater streamers. In New England, you'll only spot this warm-weather visitor during the hottest summer months in garden ponds, aquariums that have been emptied outdoors, or very occasionally in warm, sheltered waterways.

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Free-floating on water surface in perfect lettuce-like rosettes with no stems or connection to the bottom - like nature's own floating salad bowl

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Thick, soft leaves with a distinctly velvety texture that feel like suede when you touch them - pale green with prominent parallel veins running lengthwise

idTips.label: Roots
idTips.description: Feathery white roots hang down into the water like delicate underwater fringe, often several inches long and giving the plant a jellyfish-like appearance from below

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Tiny, inconspicuous white flowers hidden within the leaf rosette - so small you'll likely miss them unless you look very carefully into the center

habitat: In New England, water lettuce appears almost exclusively in artificial environments like garden ponds, water gardens, and decorative fountains where it's been introduced as an ornamental plant. Very rarely, you might find it in warm, shallow, slow-moving waters during peak summer heat, but it cannot survive our winters and dies off with the first frost.

seasonality.spring: Absent in New England - too cold for this tropical species to establish naturally.
seasonality.summer: Peak growing season when water lettuce may appear in garden ponds and warm waterways, forming dense floating mats in ideal conditions. Look for the distinctive lettuce-like rosettes during July and August heat waves.
seasonality.fall: Plants begin declining as temperatures drop, with leaves turning yellow and deteriorating. Dies completely with first frost.
seasonality.winter: Completely absent - this tropical plant cannot survive New England's freezing temperatures.

funFact: Water lettuce can reproduce so rapidly that a single plant can create enough offspring to cover an entire pond in just one growing season - which is why it's considered one of the world's most aggressive aquatic weeds in tropical climates!
confusionNotes: Most likely to be confused with young water hyacinth, but water lettuce has that distinctive velvety leaf texture and forms tighter, flatter rosettes that truly look like floating lettuce heads, while water hyacinth has shinier, more inflated leaves.
contextualKnowledge: Despite its innocent lettuce-like appearance, water lettuce is considered an invasive species and is actually prohibited in many states due to its ability to completely take over waterways in warm climates. In New England, our cold winters naturally control it, but it's still wise to dispose of aquarium or pond plants responsibly.
compareHints: Water lettuce is the only species in its genus Pistia, making it quite unique in the arum family. Unlike other arums you might know (like skunk cabbage or jack-in-the-pulpit), water lettuce is completely aquatic and lacks the distinctive spathe and spadix flower structure typical of most arum family members. Its closest relatives in the family are much more terrestrial and have very different leaf shapes and growth habits.
